articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Qatar join condemnation of Iran attack on Bahrain
articles.summary:
Saudi Arabia, Qatar join condemnation of Iran attack on Bahrain

Saudi Arabia and Qatar have joined the UAE in condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain earlier on Sunday. 

In a statement posted on X, Qatar's foreign ministry expressed its "categorical rejection of attacks on economic facilities, civilian objects and civilians, and affirms that the continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that threatens the region’s security and stability”.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, said it "affirms its full solidarity with Bahrain in all measures it takes to protect its security and stability", accusing Tehran of "undermining regional security and stability”. 

Iran attacked US military bases in both Qatar and Saudi Arabia, along with Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, Iraq and Jordan throughout the first months of the war, which began in late February. But such attacks have lulled since April amid ceasefire negotiations between Washington and Tehran. 

#Statement | The Foreign Ministry expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s condemnation and denunciation, in the strongest terms, of the heinous Iranian attacks on a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain. The Kingdom affirms its full solidarity with Bahrain in all measures it takes to protect its security and stability.

— Foreign Ministry 🇸🇦 (@KSAmofaEN) November 22, 2026

articles.title: Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
articles.summary:
Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels

The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.

The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.

The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.

At the closing plenary, Cop31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged that countries had failed to agree on the proposed document.

“We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” Kurum said.

This is a developing story. We'll bring more updates shortly.

articles.title: Cop31 talks collapse as EU and other countries reject final climate deal
articles.summary:
Cop31 talks collapse as EU and other countries reject final climate deal

Submitted by MEE staff on Sun, 11/22/2026 - 12:38
European Union, Panama and other countries reject the final proposal over its failure to explicitly address fossil fuels
Cop31 President and Turkey’s Minister of Environment Murat Kurum attends a session of the UN Climate Change Conference (Cop31) in Antalya on 22 November 2026 (AFP)
Off

The Cop31 climate summit in Turkey ended without agreement after the European Union and several countries rejected a proposed deal that failed to explicitly address fossil fuels and provide stronger financial support to developing nations.

Cop31 President Murat Kurum said that the negotiations had failed to secure consensus, adding that the proposed decisions had not been adopted.

"It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted," he told the closing plenary.

"We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a 'take it or leave it' demand."

The European Union, the Marshall Islands, Panama, Norway and Vanuatu were among those that formally objected to the proposed Antalya Pact.

The talks had been scheduled to end on Friday but continued until Sunday, as negotiators tried to resolve disagreements over the proposed agreement.

The breakdown followed more than two weeks of negotiations, making the summit the longest in the history of the UN climate conference process.

Cop31 draft agreement ‘the worst ever', campaigners warn
Read More »

Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, formally rejected the Antalya Pact, saying it failed to meet the urgency of the climate crisis.

"We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels," he said.

The dispute centred on the omission of an explicit reference to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas, despite the commitment made by countries at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.

The latest draft referred to earlier decisions, including the Dubai agreement, but did not explicitly mention fossil fuels. 

It also retained provisions on carbon capture and storage, a technology promoted by some oil-producing countries but criticised by environmental groups as a potential means of prolonging fossil fuel production.

'Moves us backwards'

The United Kingdom criticised the proposed agreement. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the summit had failed to build the consensus required for meaningful climate action.

"This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it.

"The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so," she said. 

Greta Thunberg at COP: Turkish energy shipments 'directly fuelling the genocide of Palestine'
Read More »

The UK described the text as a setback, saying: "It moves us backwards; it is the lowest common denominator when it should have been uniting us in action."

Panama also formally rejected the agreement, saying the text failed to address its demands.  

"What we cannot accept is that we are asked to drop our stance because the atmosphere does not negotiate, the planet does not negotiate," the representative said.

The Republic of the Marshall Islands also rejected the proposed agreement, warning that it threatened the security of vulnerable island nations.

"We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security," its representative said.

"Our needs are so great, but the gap keeps growing. People are dying, the seas are rising."

Norway also joined the objections, while Germany had earlier indicated that it would not accept the draft in its existing form.

articles.title: 'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
articles.summary:
'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks

Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.

Settlers attacked the villages of Deir al-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, overnight between Saturday and Sunday, setting fire to Palestinian-owned vehicles and spraying racist graffiti on homes, according to Palestinian media reports.

Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.

"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.

Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel's next government on 8 November by President Isaac Herzog.

He accused National Security Minister Ben Gvir and Finance Minister Smotrich of bringing the West Bank "to the brink of unchecked anarchy".

"This reality is not inevitable," he said, describing it as the consequence of poor leadership.

He said authorities should use all available measures, including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to stop the perpetrators.
